items.name: Congestion control
items.explanation: A sender cannot see how full the network is, so it guesses from losses and delays and slows down when it thinks a link is overloaded. Algorithms such as Reno, CUBIC and BBR make that guess differently, which changes how fast a transfer ramps up.

assumedBy.quote: we had to address two main concerns: the CPU efficiency of mvfst and the effectiveness of our primary congestion control implementation
Implementation choices can affect performance, such as efficient packet transmission and choice of congestion control algorithm.

items.name: Middleboxes
items.explanation: Firewalls, NATs and proxies sit between client and server and read or rewrite packets on the way. Once they depend on a protocol's header layout, that layout is hard to change, which is why new transports struggle to spread.

assumedBy.quote: TCP is also prone to ossification, where the protocol becomes difficult to upgrade because network middleboxes such as firewalls make assumptions about the packets’ format.

items.name: UDP
items.explanation: UDP sends single packets with no connection, no ordering and no resending of lost ones. That leaves a protocol built on top free to add exactly the reliability it wants, which is what QUIC does.

assumedBy.quote: The use of UDP allows QUIC packets to traverse middleboxes.

items.name: The NGINX worker model
items.explanation: NGINX runs several worker processes, and each request is handled start to finish by one of them. Each worker keeps its own pool of open upstream connections, so a request can only reuse a connection held by the worker it landed on.

assumedBy.quote: The NGINX worker (process) architecture has operational drawbacks for our use cases that hurt our performance and efficiency.
